refutation.note: Searched for a result that contradicts the rival (Think-SFT's 'Answer:' then value-on-next-line ending is a short-answer, easy-problem template: about 1 % of finished answers under 3,000 tokens, near 0 above 8,000; the RL delta's box removes it; grading part about 3-4 per 500 on MATH-500 and under 1 per 328 on hard328). Read after.jsonl (result-c8b994 cap 32k, result-5251c9 fresh2026: neither measures layout misses), the board list (60 newest) and result-818c20 ('16 of its 74 finished wrong answers end in a line equal to the gold ... v3 undercounts it by ~4 per sample', which matches the rival's 3-4 per 500), result-389164 ('Clean 322 and grader v4 move no share by more than 3.5 points', consistent with a small hard328 grading part), knowledge-4662c6 and knowledge-499152 (other v3 errors, not this one). The stored rows agree with the rival: duel p1 counts 16 layout rows in 1,046 short finished rows (1.5 %) and 1 in 666 long ones; offline test 1 gives 4 layout rows over 4 hard328 samples (1.0 per sample, and test 3 says only about 70 % of layout rows are blank under v3, so about 0.7 per 328 are off-line endings, i.e. 'under 1'). The weak spot: about 30 % of 'layout' rows are not off-line endings at all. The p2 example row (hard328 #272, 'Answer: $5/2', v3 extracted '$5/2', scored wrong) is a v3 parse failure on an unclosed '$'. The rival's statement covers only the off-line ending and does not claim these rows, so this is a gap in coverage, not a contradiction.

wins_judgement: Offline the theory gained +1.65 nats over 4 tests, all inside or within noise. p4 (+0.86: the hybrid's blank-extraction share of finished answers falls by 0.004 against Think-SFT's, n 548) is the one gain the mechanism earned, since 'the RL delta replaces the ending with a box' gives the sign and size. But result-284db5 (unboxed finished answers 22 -> 1) already pointed that way, and the rival makes the same claim. p3 (blank share 0.70, +0.11) was matched almost exactly by both readers (0.68, 0.65), so no reader needed the theory for it. p1 (0.036 against a predicted 0.075, at the bottom edge of the interval, +0.38) and p2 (-0.009, outside the interval and at its lower edge, +0.29) won only because the readers' intervals were wider. Both point at the rival's account: the rate is lower on long hard328 answers and higher on easy problems, not fixed per answer. The theory's own difficulty test came in on the side its fixed-rate claim forbids. There are no held-out advocate claims (heldout_claims 0, strikes 0).
rival: The rival explains every offline number at least as well, and explains p1 and p2 better (the low hard328 share and the negative difficulty gap follow from misses sitting on short answers). Duel state: loses to rival, total -3.05 nats over 2 separating tests. k1 (short minus long miss rate, measured 0.0138 [0.0072, 0.0205], n 292; theory 0.001 [-0.007, 0.009], rival 0.008 [0.002, 0.015]): gain -0.65. k2 (median length of layout rows over all finished rows, measured 0.35 [0.24, 0.44], n 20, replicated; theory 0.95 [0.6, 1.45], rival 0.55 [0.32, 0.85]): gain -2.40. k3 (within MATH-500, below minus above the median length: 0.0126, n 315) also lies above the theory's 0.008 bound. k2 separates most clearly: the layout rows are about a third the median length, not a random draw of finished answers. I read duel script rivals/r8-m09/p1.py. It follows the recipe as written: 8 files, first row per problem_index, finished = cap_hit not true and finish_reason != 'length', wrong = score_v3 != 1, candidate after the last 'Answer:' (else last non-empty line), cleaning in the stated order, agree(C, gold), Short n_new < 3000 against Long >= 8000. The bootstrap is over (bench, problem) units. Its alt reading (re-strip after each step) gives the same value.

novelty.nearest: Pitfalls of Rule- and Model-based Verifiers (Huang et al., 2505.22203): rule-based math verifiers keep >99 % precision, but recall drops to about 0.86 on average when answers are in other formats or long-tail forms. Recall is lower for long-CoT R1-Distill generators (about 0.92) and for harder datasets, so false negatives grow with model strength and difficulty.
novelty.difference: The paper puts verifier false negatives on harder problems and stronger long-CoT generators, and attributes them to equivalent-form mismatches. The rival names one specific layout (an 'Answer:' marker with the value on the next line, copied from a teacher template) that is concentrated on short answers to easy problems. That is the opposite direction from the paper. The rival also says an added RL weight delta removes the layout by boxing the ending.

import_carries_gain.which: The theory's imports are 2505.22203 (rule-verifier recall depends on generator layout and is lower for long-CoT) and 2504.07912 (correctness-reward RL collapses to one output format). Neither carries a winning claim. 2504.07912 is a general prior for p4 (the RL delta boxes the ending), but the board item result-284db5 is what supports p4. 2505.22203 implies more misses on long, hard answers, which the duel data contradict (16 short against 1 long). The theory's p1 and p2 points did not come from either import, and the wins came from the readers' wider intervals.

verdict: weak: the theory loses to the rival (duel state 'loses to rival', -3.05 nats; the short-answer template beats the fixed per-answer rate on both separating length tests), and the round folder has no forecast_scores.json, so 'stands' is excluded on two counts. No item refutes the rival's mechanism, and it is only partly published.
